question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?

then.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

question: Does the obligation to indicate that deep-fakes are artificially generated apply when prosecuting a criminal offence?

then.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?

then.answer: Not always. Falling within one of the eight Annex III use-case categories (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes) triggers the Annex III classification route in Article 6(2), but Article 6(3) allows a derogation. An Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or carries out a preparatory task to an assessment. A provider relying on the derogation must document its self-assessment before placing the system on the market and still register the system under the Article 49(2) registration duty for Annex III systems treated as not high-risk. Separately, note that Annex III is not the only route to high-risk status: under Article 6(1) a system is also high-risk where it is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation.

now.ans: Not automatically. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk only where it falls within one of the lettered use cases listed under the eight areas of Annex III, namely biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. By derogation, Article 6(3) provides that such a system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. That derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk, and the provider must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market.

question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?

then.answer: Not medium risk. The AI system is high-risk, because the AI Act does not operate a medium-risk tier for AI systems and the device's sectoral risk class does not carry across to the AI system's own classification. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and where that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex I Section A lists medical devices, so both conditions are met on the facts stated, and the classification turns on the existence of the third-party assessment rather than on the device's own risk class. Article 43(3) then folds the AI Act assessment into the sectoral third-party conformity-assessment procedure, meaning the notified body handling the medical device assessment covers both regimes in one procedure, with a new assessment required under Article 43(4) in the event of a substantial modification. As a high-risk system it must meet the Chapter III Section 2 requirements under Article 8, including the documented lifecycle risk-management system under Article 9, the data-governance and dataset quality requirements under Article 10, and the transparency and instructions-for-use duties towards deployers under Article 13, which in practice can be run alongside the ISO 14971, ISO 13485, and MDR Annex I Chapter III work already performed for the device.

now.ans: No, the AI system is not "medium risk"; it is high-risk, because the Act does not import the medical device regulation's risk classes and instead applies its own tiers. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where both conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for its placing on the market. Both limbs are satisfied here, so the AI system is high-risk irrespective of the device's own risk class, and Article 43(3) folds the AI Act conformity assessment into the sectoral notified body procedure, so the Chapter III Section 2 requirements are verified as part of the single medical device assessment.

question: Does the EU AI Act explicitly requires to use explainable AI techniques such as LIME or SHAP to increase the trustworthiness of high-risk AI systems?

then.answer: No, the EU AI Act mandates no specific explainable-AI technique such as LIME or SHAP, and Article 13 instead requires only that high-risk AI systems be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret their output. Article 14 requires effective human oversight, and Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

now.ans: No, the EU AI Act mandates no specific explainable-AI technique such as LIME or SHAP, and Article 13 instead requires only that high-risk AI systems be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret their output. Article 14 requires effective human oversight, and Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. The Act is technique-agnostic, so the choice of any interpretability method is left to the provider.

question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?

then.answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk.

now.ans: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?

then.answer: Article 5 bans an exhaustive list of practices, subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or socio-economic situation, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, and the remaining enumerated categories, and one-to-one verification against a claimed identity is not among them; the Article 5 restrictions on biometrics attach to practices such as untargeted facial-image scraping and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, which involve identifying persons without or against a claim of identity rather than authenticating one. Classification therefore falls to Article 6, whose two routes are the Annex I route, where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment, and the Annex III route, covering the eight listed use-case categories including biometrics. The biometrics category of Annex III does not capture verification systems whose sole purpose is to confirm that a natural person is who he or she claims to be, so the system is high-risk only where a separate condition is met: where it functions as a safety component of an Annex I product subject to third-party conformity assessment, or where the same system is deployed for a further purpose falling within another Annex III category, for example as part of biometric categorisation, emotion recognition, or an access, employment or law-enforcement use case listed there. Absent such a purpose, the deployer's residual duty is the Article 50 transparency regime, under which a system interacting directly with natural persons must disclose its AI nature. Two facts should be confirmed before relying on this classification: that the verification function is genuinely limited to one-to-one confirmation of a claimed identity and does not perform identification against a database of persons who have made no identity claim, and that the system is not embedded as a safety component in an Annex I regulated product.

now.ans: Biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is neither a prohibited practice nor, on that basis alone, high-risk. Article 5 bans an exhaustive list of practices, subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, individual criminal-offence risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition in the workplace and education, biometric categorisation inferring race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, and one-to-one verification is not among them. Annex III, point 1(a) classifies remote biometric identification systems as high-risk but expressly excludes AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be, so the Article 6(2) route is not engaged. The system would nonetheless be high-risk if, in fact, it is used beyond that sole verification purpose so as to fall within another Annex III use case, or if it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I under Article 6(1).

question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?

then.answer: Article 6 classifies an AI system as high-risk on two routes, and the first of those captures an AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes the Medical Devices Regulation, where that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service. Class IIa, IIb and III devices satisfy that second condition by operation of the MDR itself: unlike class I devices, which are in principle self-certified by the manufacturer, they cannot be CE-marked without notified body involvement, and the AI safety component therefore falls within Article 6(1) irrespective of its own technical sophistication or autonomy. Conformity assessment under Article 43 is then carried out under the relevant sectoral legislation, the MDR procedure with notified body involvement, rather than through the internal-control procedure of Annex VI, which is available only for Annex III systems where harmonised standards or common specifications are applied; the AI Act requirements are assessed as part of the single MDR conformity assessment rather than in a parallel procedure. Class I devices under the MDR, where no notified body is involved, fall outside the Article 6(1) route on these facts, and any high-risk status would have to be established independently on the Annex III route.

now.ans: Yes, an AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a medical device classified IIa, IIb or III under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 is high-risk. Article 6(1) treats an AI system as high-risk where both conditions are fulfilled: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service. Annex I lists the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (and the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/746), and classes IIa, IIb and III mandate notified body involvement, so both limbs are satisfied. This classification applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device.

question: What documentation does a provider of a high-risk AI system needs to keep available for the national competent authorities, and for how long?

then.answer: Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

now.ans: Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?

then.answer: Article 14 is the provision that governs human oversight. Human oversight measures also feed into the risk management system under Article 9, which requires a risk management system to be established, implemented, documented and maintained for high-risk AI systems.

now.ans: Article 14 governs human oversight, requiring that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed, including through appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use, with oversight measures commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use and built into the system by the provider or identified for implementation by the deployer. The natural persons assigned oversight must be enabled to understand the system's capacities and limitations and monitor its operation, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret its output, decide not to use the system or disregard, override or reverse its output, and intervene or interrupt the system through a stop button or similar procedure. For remote biometric identification systems under point 1(a) of Annex III, Article 14(5) adds that no action or decision may be taken by the deployer on the basis of the identification unless it has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority, except where Union or national law considers that requirement disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum purposes.

question: What is the meaning and purpose of 'testing data' in the context of AI systems, and why is it important that it is not leaked during the training process?

then.answer: Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.

now.ans: Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. It must be kept separate from the training and validation data so that this evaluation is genuinely independent. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.

question: What are the high-risk uses of AI systems listed under 'Administration of justice and democratic processes' cited in the EU AI Act?

then.answer: Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

now.ans: Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?

then.answer: Only where the model is released under a free and open-source licence and is not classified as having systemic risk. Article 53(2) exempts such providers from the Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up to date technical documentation of the model per Annex XI, and from the Article 53(1)(b) duty to make information and documentation available to downstream providers integrating the model into their AI systems per Annex XII. The exception does not cover the Article 53(1)(c) obligation to put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, nor the Article 53(1)(d) obligation to publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, for which the Commission adopted the mandatory disclosure template on 24 July 2025 covering public datasets, scraped web content, user data, synthetic data and licensed content. It also falls away entirely once the model is classified as having systemic risk under Article 51, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs or where the Commission so designates on the Annex XIII criteria, in which case the full Article 53 obligations apply alongside the Article 55 obligations on model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation at Union level, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure.

now.ans: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

question: Which AI systems used in education or vocational training should be classified as high-risk according to the EU AI Act?

then.answer: High-risk where the system falls within the education and vocational training use case listed in Annex III, which is one of the eight use-case categories that Annex III designates as high-risk. Article 6(2) classifies an AI system as high-risk on that basis alone once it falls within the use case. Article 6(3) withdraws that classification only where the system poses no significant risk of harm and performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task.

now.ans: High-risk under Article 6(2), which makes AI systems listed in Annex III high-risk, are the four education and vocational training use cases in point 3 of Annex III: systems intended to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels, systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes including where those outcomes steer the learning process, systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or be able to access, and systems intended for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests, in each case in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. By derogation under Article 6(3), such a system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, though it is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons. A provider relying on that derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service. Separately, an educational AI system is also high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment.

question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?

then.answer: Yes, a disclosure duty applies. Under Article 50(1), providers must design AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the circumstances of use. Two adjacent transparency duties in the same article may attach to the same deployment. Where the system generates synthetic content, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Where the system performs emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, Article 50(3) requires the deployer to inform the exposed natural persons and to process the personal data in accordance with the GDPR, the Law Enforcement Directive and Regulation (EU) 2018/1725, subject to the same criminal-offence carve-out and to ancillary use that is inseparable from the primary service. Article 50(4) adds deployer disclosure for deep fakes and for AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, relaxed for artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works, disapplied where use is authorised by law for criminal enforcement, and disapplied for text that has undergone human review or editorial control where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for its publication.

now.ans: Yes, a transparency duty applies: under Article 50(1) providers must design and develop AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, and the information must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first interaction and in conformity with applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). Two limits apply. No disclosure is required where the AI nature is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect natural person, taking account of the circumstances and context of use, and the obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence. Where the interacting system is an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system, Article 50(3) additionally requires the deployer to inform the natural persons exposed to it and to process personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, with the same carve-out for systems permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences under appropriate safeguards.

question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?

then.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibited practices in Article 5 attracts the highest penalty tier, namely administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). That ceiling applies to breach of any of the eight prohibitions in Article 5, which bar subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques that distort behaviour and cause significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities arising from age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, social scoring producing unjustified detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts, criminal risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial recognition databases, emotion recognition in the workplace and in education, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and real time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Article 99 requires the fine actually imposed to be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and to reflect the gravity and nature of the infringement, so the figures above are ceilings rather than fixed amounts.

now.ans: Non-compliance with the prohibited practices in Article 5 attracts the highest penalty tier under Article 99(3): administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. That ceiling applies to any of the eight prohibited practices under Article 5, namely subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, social scoring, criminal-offence risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial recognition databases, emotion recognition in the workplace and in education institutions, biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and set with regard to the gravity and nature of the infringement. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) caps the fine at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount.

question: How does Annex II relate to prohibited uses of AI systems?

then.answer: Annex II operates only as an input to one narrow exception within the prohibitions, not as a prohibition in its own right. Article 5 bans eight categories of AI practice, including subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities arising from age, disability or socio-economic situation, social scoring producing unjustified detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts, criminal-risk profiling based solely on personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images for facial recognition databases, emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Annex II lists the criminal offences that make the third law-enforcement objective under Article 5(1)(h) available, namely terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs, weapons or nuclear material, murder, kidnapping, rape, armed robbery, organised crime, participation in a criminal organisation and environmental crime, and only where the offence is punishable in the relevant Member State by a custodial sentence of at least four years.

now.ans: Annex II does not itself prohibit anything; it operates as the closed list of criminal offences that narrows one exception to a prohibited practice under Article 5, namely the ban on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes. Article 5(1)(h)(iii) permits such use only for the localisation or identification of a person suspected of an Annex II offence, and only where that offence is punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years. The Annex II offences are terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs or tissue, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Annex II is irrelevant to the other prohibited practices in Article 5, which cover subliminal or manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, predictive policing based solely on personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition at work and in education, and biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes.

question: Can the European Commission amend Annex III of the EU AI Act to add or modify use-cases classified as high-risk AI systems? Under what conditions?

then.answer: The European Commission may amend Annex III by delegated act, but only within the boundaries already fixed by the legislature: it can add or modify a use-case only inside one of the eight areas Annex III already lists (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, and the remaining listed areas), and only where that use-case poses a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. Those two conditions in Article 7(1) are cumulative, so a use-case that is serious but sits outside the eight enumerated areas cannot be added by delegated act, creating a new area requires amendment of the Act itself by the ordinary legislative procedure. In assessing whether the equivalence-of-risk condition is met, Article 7(2) obliges the Commission to weigh a fixed set of criteria: the intended purpose of the system; the extent to which it has been used or is likely to be used; the nature and amount of data processed, in particular special categories of personal data; the degree to which the system acts autonomously and the possibility of human override; the extent to which its use has already caused harm to health and safety, adversely impacted fundamental rights or given rise to significant concerns as to the likelihood of such harm, as evidenced for instance by reports to national competent authorities; the potential extent of such harm, in particular its intensity and its ability to affect a plurality of persons or to disproportionately affect a particular group; the extent to which potentially harmed persons depend on the outcome and cannot reasonably opt out of it; any imbalance of power or vulnerability of those persons vis-à-vis the deployer; the reversibility of the outcome, with outcomes affecting health, safety or fundamental rights not to be deemed reversible merely because they are technically capable of being reversed; the benefits of the system's deployment; and the extent to which existing Union law already provides effective measures of redress, excluding claims for damages. Under Article 7(3) the Commission may equally remove a use-case from Annex III where the high-risk AI systems concerned no longer pose any significant risk to fundamental rights, health or safety, assessed against the same Article 7(2) criteria, and only where the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights under Union law. Any such amendment must be adopted as a delegated act in accordance with Article 97, which subjects the empowerment to the usual safeguards, expert consultation in preparation, revocation at any time by the European Parliament or the Council, and entry into force only if neither institution objects within the prescribed period. The Article 7 power reaches only the Annex III route to high-risk classification under Article 6(2); it does not govern the Annex I route under Article 6(1), where high-risk status follows from the product being covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and requiring third-party conformity assessment. Nor does it touch Article 5: the eight categories of prohibited practice are exhaustively fixed by the legislature and cannot be widened or narrowed by delegated act, so a practice that is banned under Article 5 does not become a high-risk use-case through Annex III amendment, and a use-case added to Annex III remains a permitted practice subject to the Chapter III requirements rather than a prohibited one.

now.ans: Yes, but only within strict limits: Article 7(1) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts amending Annex III, the list of high-risk use-cases under the eight areas, by adding or modifying use-cases where two conditions are fulfilled cumulatively, namely that the AI systems are intended to be used in an area already listed in Annex III, and that they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, equivalent to or greater than that posed by the high-risk AI systems already listed there. Neither limb suffices alone, so the Commission cannot create a wholly new area, and when assessing the second limb it must weigh the criteria in Article 7(2), including the intended purpose, the extent of use, the nature and amount of data processed, the degree of autonomy, the severity and reversibility of harm, and the availability of effective measures of redress or of measures preventing or substantially minimising those risks. Article 7(3) separately allows removal of a use-case where it no longer poses any significant risk to fundamental rights, health or safety and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection under Union law. Any such delegated act must follow Article 97, under which the delegation runs for five years from 1 August 2024 with tacit extension, the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State before adoption, and the act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, extendable by a further three months.

question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?

then.answer: AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful.

now.ans: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;

question: Should market surveilance authorities be provided with remote access to documentations and data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system?

then.answer: Article 16 requires providers to keep the technical documentation (Articles 11 and 18) and the automatically generated logs (Article 19), and to demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system to competent authorities on request under Article 21, and that duty covers the data-governance records showing that the training, validation and testing data sets satisfy Article 10, meaning provenance, preparation and bias examination under Article 10(2) and 10(2)(f), and the relevance, representativeness and freedom from errors required by Article 10(3). Deployers owe a parallel duty under Article 26 to cooperate with market-surveillance authorities and to retain the logs generated by the system to the extent those logs are under their control.

now.ans: Not as a standing entitlement: the Act frames this as a duty to make documentation available on request, not to grant permanent remote access to development data sets. Providers of high-risk AI systems must draw up the technical documentation before the system is placed on the market, keep it up to date, and present it in a clear and comprehensive form enabling national competent authorities to assess conformity (Article 11), with the contents of Annex IV covering the design specifications, the system architecture and the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate the system, and datasheets describing the training methodologies and the training, validation and testing data sets, including their provenance, scope and main characteristics. Providers must in addition demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system to a competent authority upon its reasoned request (Article 16), while deployers must cooperate with the relevant competent authorities in any action taken in relation to the system (Article 26). Article 10 requires the training, validation and testing data sets themselves to be subject to appropriate data governance and management practices and to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete, but the Act does not oblige providers to give market surveillance authorities open remote access to those data sets, so any such access is a matter for the authority's specific, justified request rather than a default arrangement.

question: If a provider of a high-risk AI system confirms that the system achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity at the time of development, then no further action is required by the provider on these aspects in the future. Correct?

then.answer: No. Article 15 requires a high-risk AI system to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle, not only at the point of development, which includes continued resilience against errors, faults and inconsistencies under Article 15(4) and continued technical and organisational cybersecurity measures such as access controls, encryption and logging of access under Article 15(5). That lifecycle duty is reinforced by Article 9, which requires a risk management system that is continuously maintained and updated, including evaluation of post-market monitoring data and testing to confirm that the system performs consistently for its intended purpose, and by Article 17, under which the provider's quality management system must cover post-market monitoring and incident reporting. Article 16 additionally obliges the provider to take corrective action where the system is no longer in conformity and to demonstrate compliance to competent authorities on request.

now.ans: No. Article 15(1) requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle, so the duty is continuing rather than satisfied at a single point in development. That continuing performance must be supported by the provider's quality management system under Article 17, which covers examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and the frequency with which they are repeated, together with procedures for managing modifications to the system. Article 15(3) to (5) further require the system to remain resilient against errors, faults and inconsistencies and against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter its use, outputs or performance, supported by technical and organisational cybersecurity measures such as access controls, encryption and logging of access. The declared levels of accuracy and accuracy metrics must be stated in the instructions for use under Article 15(2) and Article 13(3)(b)(ii), including any known and foreseeable circumstances that may affect that expected level, so the provider must keep those declarations aligned with the system's actual performance over time.

question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?

then.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

now.ans: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

question: Does "systemic risk" apply to AI systems or general purpose AI models or both?

then.answer: Article 51 classifies a general-purpose AI model as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, or where the Commission so designates it on the Annex XIII criteria. That designation attaches to the model itself, and it triggers the four additional provider obligations in Article 55: model evaluation under standardised protocols including documented adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level including their sources, tracking and reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and adequate cybersecurity protection for both the model and its physical infrastructure. Providers may rely on the Article 56 codes of practice, facilitated by the AI Office, to demonstrate compliance until a harmonised standard is published. AI systems are governed by the separate risk tiers of the Regulation and are never themselves designated as carrying systemic risk, though the designation has a knock-on effect for the model provider: the Article 53(2) carve-out that relieves free and open-source GPAI models of the Annex XI technical documentation and Annex XII downstream-provider information duties falls away once a model is designated under Article 51, leaving the full Article 53 and Article 55 obligations in place regardless of licence.

now.ans: Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

question: Are AI systems that fall under one of the areas of Annex III, but not falling within a use-case within such areas, considered high-risk?

then.answer: No. Falling within one of the eight areas listed in Annex III is not by itself sufficient; the system must fall within a specific use-case described in that area. Annex III sets out its eight high-risk areas (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes) through defined use-cases, and Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk only where it falls within one of those Annex III use-cases. A system operating in an Annex III area but outside any listed use-case is therefore not high-risk on that route, though it may still be high-risk under the Annex I route in Article 6(1) where it is a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment.

now.ans: No. Annex III is structured as eight numbered areas, each containing lettered use-cases, and Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk only where it falls within one of those listed use-cases, not merely within the broader subject-matter of an area. A system operating in a field such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, or administration of justice and democratic processes, but outside every lettered entry under the relevant heading, is therefore not high-risk on the Annex III route. Such a system may still be high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Conversely, a system that does fall within a listed use-case escapes high-risk classification only through the Article 6(3) derogation, which requires no significant risk of harm plus a narrow procedural task, improvement of a previously completed human activity, detection of decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task, and never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons.

question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?

then.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

now.ans: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

question: If I have an AI system that is high-risk because listed in the use cases of Annex III, and change it to a different use case that is not in Annex I or III, does it stay high-risk due to its historical provenance?

then.answer: No. High-risk status under Article 6 attaches to the system's current intended purpose, not to its history, so a system that no longer falls within any of the eight Annex III use cases (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes) and is not a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I subject to third-party conformity assessment is not high-risk on either Article 6 route. If the system is still offered or can still reasonably be used for the original Annex III purpose, the Annex III route under Article 6(2) continues to apply.

now.ans: No, classification is not historical and does not attach to a system's provenance. Under Article 6 an AI system is high-risk only on two routes, namely where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), or where it falls within one of the listed use-cases under the eight areas of Annex III pursuant to Article 6(2). Both routes turn on the intended purpose of the system as it is placed on the market or put into service, so once the intended purpose is genuinely changed to a use case outside Annex I and Annex III, the system is no longer high-risk. The change must be real and reflected in the documented intended purpose, since a system that continues in substance to serve an Annex III use-case remains high-risk, and an Annex III system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk notwithstanding the Article 6(3) derogation for narrow procedural, result-improving, pattern-detecting or preparatory tasks.

question: How are AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum classified, and what exception is given for certain campaign-related tools?

then.answer: Under Annex III point 8(b), AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, are high-risk under Article 6(2). Annex III point 8(b) itself excludes systems to whose output natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used only to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view, which therefore fall outside this high-risk category.

now.ans: Under Annex III point 8(b), AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, are high-risk under Article 6(2). Annex III point 8(b) itself excludes systems to whose output natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used only to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view, which therefore fall outside this high-risk category.

question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?

then.answer: Article 1 sets the objective of the Regulation, which is to lay down harmonised rules for placing AI systems on the market, putting them into service, and using them in the Union. It pursues that objective through prohibitions on certain practices, requirements for high-risk AI systems, transparency obligations, rules for general-purpose AI models, and measures supporting innovation.

now.ans: The purpose of the Regulation under Article 1 is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union and supporting innovation. To that end, Article 1 lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of AI systems in the Union, prohibitions of certain AI practices, specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems, harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems, harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models, rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement, and measures to support innovation with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.

question: Under the EU AI Act, which specific AI systems are explicitly listed as high-risk because they make decisions in critical life- and health-related situations involving emergency calls and triage?

then.answer: These fall within the essential private and public services heading, one of the eight Annex III high-risk use-case categories alongside biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, law enforcement, migration asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Because classification runs through the Annex III route in Article 6(2), the Article 6(3) derogation for systems posing no significant risk is unlikely to be available, since evaluating calls or setting dispatch priority influences rather than merely prepares the human assessment.

now.ans: Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to be used for dispatching or prioritising in dispatching emergency first-response services, or for triage of emergency medical-service patients (including by fire brigades and medical aid), are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk use cases and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk. That classification triggers the Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk systems.

question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as part of their supervisory role for an AI regulatory sandbox, compliance with which specific Article must the market surveillance authority verify?

then.answer: Compliance with Article 74 must be verified. Within an AI regulatory sandbox, which each Member State must establish under Article 57 as a controlled environment for developing, training, testing, and validating innovative AI systems for a limited time before placing on the market, the authority exercises that supervisory function alongside the regulatory guidance and supervised risk mitigation the sandbox provides.

now.ans: Article 57, the provision requiring each Member State to establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox providing a controlled environment for the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before they are placed on the market or put into service under an agreed sandbox plan. Compliance verification extends to the competent authority's duties under that Article to allocate sufficient resources, to provide guidance, supervision and support with a view to identifying risks to fundamental rights, health and safety and ensuring effective mitigation measures, and to suspend testing or participation temporarily or permanently where no effective mitigation is possible. The sandbox does not affect the supervisory or corrective powers of the authorities supervising it, and the market surveillance authority designated under Article 74, which integrates enforcement of this Regulation with Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and confers full investigation and corrective powers, retains those powers in full.

question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?

then.answer: An AI system used solely to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III is not high-risk where it performs a narrow procedural or preparatory task and does not materially influence the outcome of the relevant assessment, but it is high-risk wherever that structuring in fact conditions or substitutes for the substantive decision. Article 6 does not treat Annex III listing as automatic classification: a system falling within an Annex III area escapes the high-risk tier only if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, which covers systems confined to a narrow procedural function or to preparing an assessment carried out by a human.

now.ans: Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task, it improves the result of a previously completed human activity, it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or it performs a preparatory task. Under Article 6(3), this exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons. The provider must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).

question: Is an AI system used to detect decision-making patterns or deviations for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?

then.answer: Even within an Annex III use case, Article 6(3)(c) provides that an AI system intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm and is not meant to replace or influence a previously completed human assessment without proper human review. However, under Article 6(3) such a system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

now.ans: Not automatically. Even within an Annex III use case, Article 6(3)(c) provides that an AI system intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm and is not meant to replace or influence a previously completed human assessment without proper human review. However, under Article 6(3) such a system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

question: Regarding the European Artificial Intelligence Board: (1) Who designates its members? (2) How long is the term? How many times is the term renewable? (3) must members represent stakeholder interests or act impartially/objectively? (4) what voting threshold is required to adopt the Board's rules of procedure (is a simple 50%+1 majority enough)?

then.answer: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

now.ans: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?

then.answer: Article 101, which empowers the Commission acting through the AI Office to impose fines on providers of general-purpose AI models of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for breaches of the Chapter V obligations, for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, or for failing to comply with a Commission request for measures, subjects those fining decisions to review by the Court of Justice of the European Union with unlimited jurisdiction rather than to annulment review alone.

now.ans: Unlimited jurisdiction. Under Article 101, which empowers the Commission to fine providers of general-purpose AI models up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for breaches of Chapter V obligations, for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, or for failing to comply with a requested measure, the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review a Commission decision fixing such a fine. The Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed. That review sits alongside the procedural safeguards in the same Article, under which the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard before adopting the decision, and any fine must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Does the provider need to recall and suspend the use of the system without undue delay, or does the MSA provide a timeframe within which the provider can take corrective actions? Or does this depend on the gravity of the situation?

then.answer: The trigger is Article 6: a provider may conclude under Article 6(3) that a system falling within an Annex III use-case category does not pose a significant risk of harm and is therefore not high-risk, but that self-assessment is documented and rebuttable, and the classification itself is fixed by Article 6(1), (2), a safety component of, or a product covered by, the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment, or a system falling within one of the eight Annex III categories (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, and the remainder of that list). Where the authority finds the derogation was wrongly invoked, the system is high-risk from that determination and the full Chapter III provider obligations attach, including, among those identified here, the risk management system under Article 9, and Article 50 transparency duties continue to apply in parallel where the system interacts directly with natural persons. Nothing in the facts engages Article 5: the exhaustively listed prohibited practices, including real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement outside the three permitted law-enforcement objectives, operate as an outright ban with no corrective-action window, and must not be conflated with the high-risk tier under Article 6, where compliance, not cessation, is the remedy.

now.ans: The market surveillance authority sets the timeframe; immediate recall and suspension is not the default. Under Article 80, which governs AI systems classified by the provider as non-high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, an authority that finds on evaluation that the system is in fact high-risk must without undue delay require the provider to bring the system into compliance and to take appropriate corrective action within a period the authority may prescribe, and failure to comply within that period exposes the provider to fines and triggers the provisional measures under Article 79(5) to (9), including prohibition, restriction, withdrawal or recall. The prescribed period is calibrated to the gravity of the case: where the system also presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, Article 79 requires corrective action, withdrawal or recall within a period the authority prescribes and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period set by the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. Independently of any authority deadline, Article 20 obliges a provider that considers or has reason to consider that its high-risk AI system is not in conformity to immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw, disable or recall it as appropriate, and to inform distributors and, where applicable, deployers, the authorised representative and importers.

question: Under the EU AI Act, what presumption applies when a high-risk AI system is trained and tested on data that reflects the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used?

then.answer: A presumption of conformity with the data-governance requirement in Article 10(4) applies. Under Article 42(1), a high-risk AI system trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used is presumed to comply with that requirement, which forms part of the broader Article 10 data-governance regime requiring training, validation and testing data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, and to be examined for possible biases. The presumption is confined to that data-governance point and does not extend to the other Chapter III obligations, such as the Article 9 risk-management system, the Article 13 transparency and instructions-for-use duties, or the Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirements.

now.ans: Such systems are presumed to comply with Article 10(4), which requires data sets to take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting within which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. This presumption is established by Article 42(1), which sets out presumptions of conformity for high-risk AI systems. The presumption extends only to Article 10(4) and does not cover the remaining data governance duties of Article 10, such as the data governance and management practices under Article 10(2) or the relevance, representativeness, error-freedom and completeness criteria of Article 10(3). Article 42(2) adds a separate presumption, under which high-risk AI systems certified, or for which a statement of conformity has been issued, under a cybersecurity scheme pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/881 with references published in the Official Journal are presumed to comply with the cybersecurity requirements of Article 15 in so far as that certificate or statement covers them.

question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.

then.answer: The required content is fixed by Annex VIII, Section A, which lists the information a provider must submit and thereafter keep up to date when registering a high-risk AI system, and the submission must be made before the system is placed on the market or put into service under Article 49(1). The registration is entered in the EU database for high-risk AI systems that the Commission sets up and manages under Article 71, which holds a publicly accessible section and a restricted-access section and keeps the data machine-readable, navigable and searchable. The items to be submitted are. The name, address and contact details of the provider. The name, address and contact details of the authorised representative, where applicable. The AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability of the system. A description of the intended purpose of the AI system and of the components and functions supported through it. A basic and concise description of the information used by the system, meaning its data and inputs, and of its operating logic. The status of the AI system, namely on the market or in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, or recalled. Article 35 is what makes that identifier meaningful, since the Commission assigns each notified body a single identification number and publishes an up-to-date list of notified bodies with their numbers and notified activities.

now.ans: A provider must enter the Section A data set of Annex VIII in the EU database before the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, Article 49(1) imposing that registration duty on the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative, and Article 71(2) assigning entry of Sections A and B of Annex VIII to them. The required items are the name, address and contact details of the provider, the same details of any person submitting the information on the provider's behalf, the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative where applicable, the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability, a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported through the system, a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic, the status of the AI system (on the market or in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, recalled), the details of the certificate issued by the notified body together with a scanned copy of that certificate where applicable, the Member States in which the system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity drawn up under Article 47, electronic instructions for use, and an optional URL for additional information. Electronic instructions for use are not submitted for high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III, and for those systems Article 49(4) confines registration to a secure non-public section of the database covering only Section A points 1 to 10 with the exception of points 6, 8 and 9. A provider that concludes under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk must still register itself and that system under Article 49(2), submitting instead the Section B information, and systems falling under point 2 of Annex III are registered at national level under Article 49(5).

question: Under the EU AI Act, what is an "AI regulatory sandbox"? Provide the definition elements (what it is, who sets it up, for whom it is intended, to do what, for how long).

then.answer: The AI Office shall make publicly available a list of planned and existing sandboxes and keep it up to date in order to encourage more interaction in the AI regulatory sandboxes and cross-border cooperation.

now.ans: ‘AI regulatory sandbox’ means a controlled framework set up by a competent authority which offers providers or prospective providers of AI systems the possibility to develop, train, validate and test, where appropriate in real-world conditions, an innovative AI system, pursuant to a sandbox plan for a limited time under regulatory supervision;

question: Under the EU AI Act, what transparency obligation applies to deployers when they use an AI system to generate or manipulate text for the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, and what are the two exceptions where this obligation does not apply?

then.answer: Under Article 50(4), a deployer that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(4), that disclosure duty does not apply in two cases: first, where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; and second, where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

now.ans: Under Article 50(4), a deployer that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(4), that disclosure duty does not apply in two cases: first, where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; and second, where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?

then.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system.
